title: A Second Wall Blocks Late-Time Fixes to the Hubble Tension
hook: Tweaking dark energy in the recent universe was already a hard way out of the Hubble tension. A new bound says it buys you 2% of the 8% you need.
key_points: The known 'normalization wall': baryon acoustic oscillations pin the product H₀ × sound horizon.
The authors add a 'shape wall' — data also constrain the *shape* of the expansion history E(z).
With the acoustic scale fixed, raising H₀ demands an equal fractional change in a distance integral.
Reconstructing E(z) from Pantheon+ supernovae and DESI DR2 BAO caps the H₀ gain at ≲2%.
Resolving the tension needs ≳8%, and the wall stands even alongside early-universe new physics.
content_html: Cosmology's most stubborn discrepancy is the Hubble tension: the early universe and the nearby universe disagree about how fast space is expanding today. One popular escape route is to change physics late — to tinker with dark energy in the recent past, leaving the early universe untouched. Miguel Sabogal, Luis Escamilla, Davide Pedrotti, Edvig Selimaj and Sunny Vagnozzi argue that route runs into a second barrier nobody had quantified.
extra_html: The familiar obstacle is a "normalization wall": measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations — the imprint of primordial sound waves used as a cosmic ruler — constrain the product of H₀ and that ruler's length, so you can't simply slide H₀ upward. The authors point out that the data also constrain the shape of the expansion history, captured by E(z) = H(z)/H₀. Holding the ruler and the acoustic angular scale fixed, they show that any fractional increase in H₀ must be matched by an equal fractional increase in the dimensionless distance integral ∫dz/E(z). Reconstructing E(z) without assuming a model — using Gaussian processes on unanchored Pantheon+ supernovae and DESI DR2 BAO data — they find the most H₀ can rise is about 2%, against the roughly 8% the tension demands. Their conclusion: late-time modifications face a percent-level "shape wall" on top of the old normalization wall, and it holds even if the early universe is modified too.

related.title: The Hubble Tension: Cosmology's Stubborn Crisis
related.hook: Two trustworthy ways of measuring how fast the universe expands keep disagreeing — and a decade of cross-checks has only hardened the gap into a genuine crisis.

related.title: Is Dark Energy Changing Over Time?
related.hook: For decades dark energy looked like a constant. New galaxy-survey data hints it may evolve — and that would shift even our measured value of the cosmic expansion rate.

related.title: Dark Energy Survives a Major Challenge
related.hook: A bold claim said the universe's accelerating expansion was an illusion. Astronomers checked the math, found the mistakes — and cosmic acceleration came out as strong as ever.

related.title: The Expanding Universe
related.hook: Distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it flees — not because they're moving through space, but because space itself is stretching.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'shape wall' this paper adds to the Hubble-tension debate?

choices.text: A limit from how the expansion rate varies with redshift, not just its overall scale
A limit from the physical size of the sound horizon at baryon drag
A limit from the angular resolution of current supernova surveys

flashcards.explanation_html: The older "normalization wall" comes from BAO pinning H₀ × r_d. The shape wall comes from relative-distance data constraining E(z) = H(z)/H₀ — the shape of the expansion history.

flashcards.prompt: How much of the needed H₀ increase can late-time modifications supply, per this analysis?
flashcards.back_html: At most about 2%, against the roughly 8% required to close the tension — so late-time tweaks alone fall well short, even when early-universe new physics is also allowed.

flashcards.prompt: Why does fixing the acoustic angular scale make raising H₀ so hard?

choices.text: Any fractional rise in H₀ must be matched by an equal fractional rise in the distance integral ∫dz/E(z)
It forces dark energy to behave exactly like a cosmological constant
It removes supernovae from the analysis entirely

flashcards.explanation_html: With r_d and θ_s held fixed, the authors show δH₀/H₀ ≈ δI/I. Data on the shape of E(z) then limit how much that integral can move — and therefore how much H₀ can rise.
